clue.text: "Big brother" couturier holding copyright on trash

indicators.note: the designer's name holds the other pieces within it, as if gripping them

parts.note: Christian Dior was a famous French fashion designer
C is the standard abbreviation for copyright, as in the circled C symbol
tat is cheap, worthless rubbish

explanation.surface: A fashion designer is grasping the rights to some rubbish, under an Orwellian gaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big brother' in quotation marks points to Orwell's all-seeing ruler, a tyrant figure; 'on' simply sets C before TAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Brother in Orwell's novel is the archetypal all-powerful tyrant, so the quoted phrase stands for an autocrat.

clue.text: Failure of French coup

parts.note: de is the French word for of
a coup is a brilliant achievement, a feat

explanation.surface: A French coup d'etat that came to nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A defeat is a loss or lack of success in a contest, a failure.

clue.text: Meeting place after iron's last pitch over river

indicators.note: in a down clue the earlier pieces sit above the river

parts.note: an iron is a golf club

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word pitch is wanted

parts.note: the Ouse is a river in Yorkshire, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A golfer heads for the bar once the last shot with the iron is played.
explanation.walkthrough: The golfing picture makes 'pitch' look like a shot; only its last letter H is used. 'after' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A clubhouse is the building where members of a sports club gather and socialise.

clue.text: European city's a new sort of dope

parts.note: a twerp is a silly person, one kind of dope or fool

explanation.surface: A newly invented kind of drug is named after a Belgian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' suggests drugs, but here it means a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Antwerp is a large port city in Belgium.

clue.text: 'Grandad', for some, a treasured record?

explanation.surface: A grandfather who is himself a much-loved old disc.
explanation.definitionFit: An oldie is informal for an elderly person, such as a grandad, and also for an old, popular song or recording.

clue.text: Onset of sudden agony gripping radius

definitions.text: Onset of sudden agony gripping radius

indicators.note: the onset is the beginning, so just the first letter of sudden is used
the word for agony wraps around the abbreviation as though clutching it

parts.note: agony is intense pain
R is the standard abbreviation for radius in geometry

explanation.surface: A sharp pain suddenly seizes the forearm bone.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a description of a wrist injury, where sudden agony grips the radius, a forearm bone.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrenched wrist ligament brings a sudden sharp pain around the radius, the bone near the wrist.

clue.text: Bridge — a card game

explanation.surface: Two card games named side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A pontoon is a floating bridge supported on boats or drums, and also the card game known elsewhere as twenty-one or blackjack.

clue.text: Good excuse for party in first-class

indicators.note: the party is placed inside the term for first-class

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written here as the letters A and I
Lib is short for the Liberal party

explanation.surface: A handy excuse for skipping a party in first-class travel.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first-class) is read as the letters AI.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a plea that one was elsewhere, used as an excuse.

clue.text: Bill admitting new senator is rubbish

indicators.note: letting someone in, so the word for bill takes the other pieces inside

parts.note: a bird's bill or beak is jokingly a nose

explanation.surface: A bill that lets in a new senator is dismissed as garbage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' suggests a piece of legislation; it is a beak, i.e. NOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense is foolish talk or ideas, much like rubbish.

clue.text: Climate may be nice, perhaps, ignoring start of year

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters are a possible rearrangement
leaving something out, so a letter is removed from the fodder
only the first letter of year is meant

explanation.surface: Weather could turn out pleasant, except at the turn of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring' drops Y from MAYBE, leaving MABE; 'perhaps' rearranges MABE plus NICE into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambience means the mood or atmosphere of a place, its prevailing climate.

clue.text: Time for 'doctor who'?

parts.note: the time-travelling Doctor of the television series roams through time, which physicists treat as an extra dimension beyond the three of space

explanation.surface: Is it time for the TV show to come on?
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Who is a long-running British TV series about a time-travelling alien.
explanation.definitionFit: In relativity, time is treated as an extra dimension added to length, breadth and height.

clue.text: Within reach, I even succeed

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: Encouragement: it is within reach, so even I can make it.
explanation.definitionFit: To achieve is to accomplish or attain an aim, to succeed in it.

clue.text: Love that is rock solid inside

indicators.note: the scrambled word is placed within the abbreviation
to rock is to shake about, so the letters of solid are jumbled

explanation.surface: Love, that is, stays rock solid on the inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock' looks like part of 'rock solid', but it is the anagram signal: SOLID shaken up gives DOLIS, which 'inside' places within IE.
explanation.definitionFit: To idolise is to adore or worship someone, a strong form of love.

clue.text: Works outing taking in politician's initiative

indicators.note: the rearranged word takes the politician inside it
works as a verb means operates on or shapes, so outing is reworked

parts.note: MP stands for Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A company day out shows a politician's enterprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works outing' looks like a staff trip; 'Works' rearranges OUTING to GUTION, which takes in MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Gumption is resourcefulness and get-up-and-go, the same as initiative.

clue.text: Mince came with rice pudding

indicators.note: to mince is to chop finely, so the letters are cut up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Minced meat served with rice pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mince' looks like the meat; it rearranges CAME plus RICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice cream is a frozen dessert, and pudding is the British word for dessert.

clue.text: Freezes digits losing ends of finger

indicators.note: losing means some letters are taken away

parts.note: digits are numbers
the end of the word finger is its final pair of letters

explanation.surface: Cold weather freezes fingers until the tips go dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freezes' is the verb: numbs, makes insensible.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold numbs the flesh, freezing it so it loses feeling.

clue.text: Have second start after working?

parts.note: read as taking on another job that begins once the usual working day is over

explanation.surface: Should I start again after work?
explanation.definitionFit: To moonlight is to hold a second job, typically in the evenings after one's main employment.

clue.text: Not all blubber's palatable and easy to swallow

indicators.note: not all of the word is used, so its final letter goes

parts.note: to blubber is to cry noisily
palatable food is edible

explanation.surface: Whale fat is not wholly appetising or easy to get down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blubber' suggests whale fat; it is the verb to weep, CRY, cut to CR.
explanation.definitionFit: Credible means believable, and a believable story is one that is easy to swallow.

clue.text: First woman attached to army unit — official

indicators.note: joined on behind, so the woman's name follows the army unit

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
in the Bible Eve was the first woman

explanation.surface: The first female soldier joins an army unit as an official.
explanation.walkthrough: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a local magistrate or steward in medieval England, a kind of official.

clue.text: Connoisseur of grand, classy case of rosé

parts.note: epic means grand or heroic in scale
U means upper-class in British slang

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An expert in grand vintages admires a smart crate of pink wine.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class (as in 'U and non-U') is British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicure is a person with refined taste in food and wine, a gourmet.

clue.text: Discharge from jet once I break down

indicators.note: to break down is to fall apart, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Discharge from a jet engine once I break down.
explanation.definitionFit: Ejection is the act of throwing out or expelling something, a discharge.

clue.text: Ground exercise protecting the queen

indicators.note: the word for exercise surrounds and shields the queen

parts.note: to train is to exercise
ER is the royal cipher, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Drills on the parade ground guard the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrain is a stretch of land considered for its physical features, ground.

clue.text: A society bird's behind

parts.note: the tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A socialite bird's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' looks like a noun for a bottom; it means at the back of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern means towards or at the back of a ship, behind it.

clue.text: Pile of papers — tramp's holding first issue

indicators.note: the tramp holds the letter within him

parts.note: a dosser is a vagrant or tramp in British slang

indicators.note: only the first letter of issue is wanted

explanation.surface: A vagrant clutches the first copy of a magazine among his papers.
explanation.walkthrough: DOSSER, British slang for a homeless person, holds I.
explanation.definitionFit: A dossier is a collection of documents about a person or subject, a file of papers.

clue.text: Material increase, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken rather than spelled

parts.note: a surge is a sudden increase

explanation.surface: A significant rise in fabric prices, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Serge is a hard-wearing twilled woollen fabric.

clue.text: Rugby losing guy in man's game

indicators.note: the shortened word goes within the word for man's

parts.note: read as male's, the plural form males

indicators.note: losing means the letters of guy are struck out of rugby wherever they fall

explanation.surface: Rugby without a certain player becomes just a man's game.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of GUY are not in order inside RUGBY, so 'losing' strikes them out wherever they sit, leaving RB; 'in' puts that inside MALES (man's read as male's).
explanation.definitionFit: Marbles is a children's game played by rolling small glass balls.

clue.text: Decent mark on spoken test

parts.note: M stands for the mark, the old German currency
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A good mark on the oral exam.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts M above ORAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Moral means ethically good, or decent.

clue.text: Area of high risk, allegedly

parts.note: a stretch of the Atlantic notorious in legend for ships and planes vanishing, though the danger is disputed

explanation.surface: A danger zone, so they say.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bermuda Triangle is a region of the western Atlantic with a supposed reputation for mysterious disappearances.

clue.text: Regular on the Spanish team

indicators.note: the regular word is placed after the Spanish article

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for the
even means regular or steady

explanation.surface: A regular player in the Spanish side.
explanation.walkthrough: A football or cricket side has eleven players, so the number stands for a team.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven is the number of players in a football or cricket side, hence a team.

clue.text: Seafood? Large amount on board

indicators.note: the large amount is added on to the board

parts.note: a plank is a board of wood
a ton, informally, is a lot

explanation.surface: A large quantity of fish is loaded onto the deck.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'Seafood' as food found in the sea, eaten by whales, not fish on a plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Plankton are tiny organisms drifting in the ocean, the staple diet of many marine animals.
